doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

title: Bix, Italians in New Orleans and Ken Burns' Jazz
summary: On Bix's standing, Sudhalter, Nick LaRocca and Italians in New Orleans, and his criticism of Ken Burns for leaning on Wynton and Crouch over Schuller.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: I guess. Do you think Bix is put higher up on a pedestal because he is one of the few white innovators, or do you even consider him an innovator?

Oh he was — the stuff was great. I mean Sudhalter makes a great case in his book, you know, about the whites. And even Nick LaRocca — you know there are more Italians down in New Orleans at the turn of the twentieth century, at the beginning of the twentieth century, than there were in New York City, even though we all came through Ellis Island. Because the French owned it, the Spanish, and then the French a second time. Catholic. And in New Orleans a similar atmosphere, weather. And there were all these Italians there. Thousands of Italians. And LaRocca always said that — he took them to task. He said they never gave the Italians enough credit for what we did, all right? They were great players. Opera. I know the first opera houses were in the Creole section in America. But great players. And you know when I saw the history, Ken Burns jazz was correct. Ken Burns’ vision of jazz. And he didn’t use enough, in terms of historical

stuff, of Gunther Schuller. Schuller had it right. He was using a little too much of Wynton and, at the time Gary Giddons, but especially Stanley Crouch. I call him Stanley Grouch. I brought him up here. What a pain in the neck, but what a funny guy.
